summary: Provides the obsoleted IPv6-specific MIB modules so repositories can be updated, noting that newer IP-MIB, TCP-MIB, UDP-MIB and IP-FORWARD-MIB handle both IPv4 and IPv6.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC marks older IPv6-only management modules as obsolete and points readers to newer modules. The newer modules can describe both IPv4 and IPv6 information.

questions: why were rfc 2465 and 2466 made historic
why were the ipv6 mib rfc documents made historic
subtitle: Why five IPv6-only MIB modules are republished with obsolete status and their RFCs made Historic.

tldr.problem: MIB repositories still contained IPv6-only modules even after updated MIBs could represent IPv4 and IPv6 in shared tables.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8096 republishes the old modules with their objects marked obsolete and reclassifies the RFCs containing them as Historic.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8096 obsoletes RFCs 2452, 2454, 2465, and 2466. The combined IP, TCP, UDP, and forwarding MIB modules are the replacements named in the RFC.

today: RFC 8096 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 2452, RFC 2454, RFC 2465, and RFC 2466. It reclassifies those four RFCs as Historic; the unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes RFC 8096.

sections.title: Why the Modules Were Republised
sections.content:
Updated IP-MIB, UDP-MIB, TCP-MIB, and IP-FORWARD-MIB modules use the InetAddressType and InetAddress construct to handle IPv4 and IPv6 in the same tables. Earlier RFCs contained IPv6-specific MIB modules, but the extracted modules in repositories had not been marked obsolete.

RFC 8096 republishes those modules with their Structure of Management Information status changed to obsolete. The RFC calls this an unusual step taken because the old modules and their RFC status created an unclear situation for repository users.
sections.plainLanguage: The newer MIB modules can describe both IPv4 and IPv6. This RFC marks the older IPv6-only modules as obsolete so repositories show that change clearly.

sections.title: The Five Republished Modules
sections.content:
The RFC republishes five modules: IPV6-TC, IPV6-MIB, IPV6-ICMP-MIB, IPV6-UDP-MIB, and IPV6-TCP-MIB. They contain textual conventions and management objects for IPv6, including interface, address, forwarding, ICMP, UDP, and TCP information.

The modules are included so MIB repositories can update their copies. Their objects have obsolete status and descriptions that identify replacement objects or groups where the RFC specifies them.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC includes five older IPv6 management modules. Each object is marked obsolete, and its description points to a replacement when one is specified.

sections.title: Replacement Objects and Tables
sections.content:
The descriptions name replacements in the newer MIB modules. For example, the old forwarding control object is replaced by IP-MIB::ipv6IpForwarding, the default hop-limit object by IP-MIB::ipv6IpDefaultHopLimit, and the interface table by IP-MIB::ipv6InterfaceTable.

Other replacements use shared tables such as IF-MIB for interface information and IP-FORWARD-MIB for forwarding entries. Some old objects have no direct replacement; the RFC explains how one value can be derived from a newer table.
sections.plainLanguage: The old objects point to replacement objects in newer MIB modules. Some replacements use shared interface or forwarding tables rather than IPv6-only tables.

sections.title: Historic Status for the Earlier RFCs
sections.content:
RFC 8096 reclassifies RFCs 2452, 2454, 2465, and 2466 as Historic. Those RFCs contain the earlier IPv6 TCP, UDP, general, textual-convention, and ICMPv6 MIB material.

The RFC also updates IANA's SMI Numbers registry with Historic annotations and revised references for entries associated with the old modules.
sections.plainLanguage: The four RFCs that originally published these IPv6-specific modules are now Historic. Registry entries also receive notes reflecting that status.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the republished objects are obsolete and should not be implemented; implementations that already use them can remove them. On that basis, it says this document has no security implications.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says implementations should not use the obsolete objects. Removing them can improve security if they created a security issue.

viz.caption: THE FIVE IPV6-ONLY MODULES REPRINTED AS OBSOLETE
